summary: Venezuela closed crossings with Colombia on 12–13 December 2016 during the withdrawal of a banknote, citing currency smuggling. Pedestrian passage resumed on 20 December at six border posts. Colombia subsequently confirmed limited overnight freight access, but the pedestrian reopening did not establish when normal vehicle and cargo movements resumed.

verification.notes: Retained uncertain onset and separated pedestrian reopening from later freight permission.

summary: Venezuela closed the Santa Elena de Uairén–Pacaraima crossing with Brazil on 13 December 2016, citing currency smuggling. Registered Brazilian vehicles could return to Brazil from 19 December, and pedestrians could cross in both directions from 20 December. Broader movement of people, cars and goods was reported restored on 6 January 2017, following these earlier partial reopenings.

verification.notes: Vehicle return exception, pedestrian endpoint and later normalization kept distinct.

summary: Venezuela closed the Santa Elena de Uairén–Pacaraima crossing with Brazil in February 2019 during the confrontation over opposition-backed humanitarian aid. The closure was announced on 21 February and reported in operation from 22 February. Formal passage resumed on 10 May, when UNHCR observed arrivals into Brazil; people had continued to use informal trails during the closure.

verification.notes: Preserved order/enforcement date range and continuing informal crossings.

summary: Venezuela stopped ordinary pedestrian passage across the Simón Bolívar and Francisco de Paula Santander bridges to Colombia on 22–23 February 2019 during the confrontation over humanitarian aid. Students, medical patients and some other vulnerable people received humanitarian access from March. Ordinary pedestrian movement resumed on both bridges on 8 June, while separate vehicle restrictions continued.

verification.notes: Named bridges and humanitarian exceptions retained; vehicle restrictions not ended by pedestrian reopening.

summary: Ecuador ordered a halt to entry by international land passenger transport during the COVID-19 emergency, covering foreign passengers from late 15 March 2020 and Ecuadorian passengers from late 16 March. Vehicle and pedestrian passage through Rumichaca, on the Colombian border, was restored on 17 December 2021. Freight and other crossings followed different arrangements, and the evidence does not establish one uninterrupted closure across all Ecuadorian land borders between those dates.

verification.notes: Separated cohort-specific orders from Rumichaca reopening; no nationwide continuous duration inferred.

summary: Paraguay restricted entry by nonresident foreigners from 16 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, initially exempting nationals, residents, authorised personnel and freight. Access resumed at three crossings with Brazil on 15 October, although the Friendship Bridge initially admitted vehicles only during specified hours. Tourist entry at designated points was permitted from 21 October, followed by pedestrian and round-the-clock permission at the Friendship Bridge from 30 October.

verification.notes: Preserved initial exemptions and distinct October vehicle, tourist and pedestrian permissions.

summary: Guatemala restricted ordinary foreign passenger entry through its land borders from the night of 16–17 March 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response. Nationals, qualifying residents and diplomats could enter under quarantine rules, while freight and authorised departures remained possible. Authorities reported the land crossings reopened on 18 September with health conditions; contemporary reports documented passengers and vehicles at Valle Nuevo and El Carmen.

verification.notes: Inbound scope, exempt travellers, freight and observed reopening locations retained.

summary: El Salvador restricted entry by nonexempt foreign travellers from 11 March 2020 in response to COVID-19. Salvadoran nationals, residents and diplomats were initially admitted subject to quarantine. Foreign land arrivals with PCR tests were documented at Las Chinamas on 21 September, establishing reopening there; the evidence does not independently confirm the same day’s operation at every border post.

verification.notes: Scoped actual September endpoint to Las Chinamas and retained initial exceptions.

summary: Colombia closed its authorised land and river crossings with Venezuela to ordinary passenger movement from 14 March 2020 to contain COVID-19. Freight and specified exceptional journeys remained permitted under rules that changed during the restriction. Colombia authorised gradual reopening from 2 June 2021; this was a change in Colombian policy, rather than confirmation that every crossing reopened on both sides that day.

verification.notes: Used operative 2 June date and distinguished policy permission from bilateral operation.

summary: The Moleson Creek–South Drain ferry between Guyana and Suriname suspended ordinary passenger service from 14 March 2020 following Suriname’s first COVID-19 case. A special repatriation trip took place during the suspension. Regular service resumed on 21 February 2021 for Guyanese and Surinamese nationals, with health requirements and limited operating days; diplomatic residents could be accommodated on request, but general foreign tourism was not restored.

verification.notes: Repatriation exception and nationality-limited regular service endpoint preserved.

summary: Suriname restricted crossings over the Maroni River from French Guiana from 14 March 2020 during the COVID-19 outbreak. Essential and authorised journeys continued, alongside informal crossings. Rules still limited waterborne travel to goods and essential passengers in July 2021; by April 2022, wider land entry from French Guiana was permitted subject to health conditions, although the exact first relaxation for ordinary visitors is uncertain.

verification.notes: Suriname onset separated from French rules; later permission is an outer bound, not exact ferry reopening.

summary: Honduras suspended ordinary passenger entry and departure through its land borders from the night of 15–16 March 2020 to contain COVID-19, while allowing freight and supplies. Immigration authorities reported a gradual reopening from 19 October, with preregistration, health checks and restricted operating hours. International bus services resumed under separate arrangements, and operation at every individual crossing was not independently documented.

verification.notes: Retained authority-reported reopening and continuing freight; did not infer every gate operation.

summary: Peru ordered international passenger transport, including land and river journeys, suspended from late 16 March 2020 during the COVID-19 emergency, exempting freight. Later rules restricted land entry by nonresident foreigners while permitting residents and specified essential travellers. Those restrictions varied by neighbouring country in December 2021 and were repealed from 14 February 2022; the documented legal changes do not establish when every crossing physically reopened.

verification.notes: Initial order and later legal phases distinguished without asserting continuous national operation.

summary: Argentina restricted entry by nonresident foreigners from 16 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission, with exceptions for freight crews, medical transport and authorised essential or humanitarian journeys. Ordinary foreign tourist entry was permitted again from 1 November 2021 through designated safe corridors. Neighbouring-country visitors and other eligible groups had received earlier permissions, and individual land crossings did not necessarily reopen together.

verification.notes: Residual ordinary tourist cohort excludes earlier neighbouring-country and special permissions.

summary: Colombia closed its land and river frontiers with Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Brazil to ordinary passenger movement from 17 March 2020 as a COVID-19 measure. Freight, exceptional journeys and later humanitarian arrangements remained possible. Colombia lifted this policy from 19 May 2021, but neighbouring countries’ rules and the availability of individual routes could still limit passage.

verification.notes: Legal dates separated from reciprocal operation; land/river scope only, no Panama road implied.

summary: Uruguay restricted entry from Argentina from 17 March 2020 during the COVID-19 emergency, while exempting citizens, residents, freight and authorised essential journeys. Restrictions on ordinary nonresident visitors continued under subsequent national rules, with exceptions added over time. From 1 November 2021, vaccinated or qualifying recovered foreigners and minors could enter; this did not remove every entry condition or establish unrestricted admission for unvaccinated adults.

verification.notes: Original March 17 onset distinguished from later March 30 policy segment; November cohort limits retained.

summary: Panama initially barred nonresident foreign land arrivals for 17 March–7 April 2020 as part of its COVID-19 response. Nationals, qualifying residents, certain dependent children and approved freight crews could still enter. The scheduled end was not a confirmed reopening: later official statistics establish foreign tourist arrivals at Paso Canoas during 2021, but do not identify the first return of ordinary tourists.

verification.notes: Scheduled expiry not treated as reopening; used annual tourist access evidence without exact date.

summary: Chile restricted foreign land entry from 18 March 2020 to curb COVID-19, initially exempting citizens and residents and allowing departures. Reopening proceeded unevenly: conditional foreign admission was authorised at four southern crossings in December 2021, but reciprocal access differed, and Los Libertadores reopened in January 2022. By 1 May 2022, the government reported 22 of 40 land complexes operating; these stages do not describe a single nationwide reopening.

verification.notes: Preserved distinction between December permission, actual crossing access and May expansion.

summary: Costa Rica restricted ordinary foreign land entry from late 18 March 2020 in response to COVID-19, while retaining access for citizens, residents, specified exempt travellers and freight. It permitted visa-exempt tourists to return from 5 April 2021 under health requirements, with arrivals reported at Peñas Blancas and Paso Canoas. Visa-required visitors and organised migrant transit remained subject to separate rules.

verification.notes: Scoped April easing to visa-exempt visitors; arrival totals are not exclusively tourist counts.

summary: Brazil restricted foreign land arrivals from eight neighbours on 19 March 2020 during the COVID-19 emergency: Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia, French Guiana, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru and Suriname. Citizens, qualifying residents, freight and specified official, humanitarian and local journeys were exempt. Wider conditional land entry was permitted by 9 December 2021, following earlier exceptions and local relaxations whose timing differed across the frontiers.

verification.notes: Eight-frontier policy excludes separate Uruguay/Venezuela orders; December date is later legal bound.

summary: French authorities restricted ordinary passenger entry from Brazil into French Guiana in March 2020 to contain COVID-19, while preserving freight and specified exempt journeys. A broader restriction at the Saint-Georges–Oiapoque road bridge followed in late June. The bridge reopened on 18 December 2021; informal river crossings and authorised travel had continued, and Brazilian entry rules followed a separate timetable.

verification.notes: Earlier March restriction separated from broadened June bridge phase; direction and exemptions retained.

summary: Bolivia ordered foreign land entry suspended for 20–31 March 2020 during the COVID-19 emergency, exempting returning citizens, residents, official missions and international freight drivers. Later rules retained restrictions while allowing additional exceptions and coordinated local border movements. By 1 December, foreign land entry was permitted under health protocols, but the initial scheduled expiry does not establish reopening in March or continuous closure until December.

verification.notes: Ordered window, September local exceptions and later December permission kept distinct.

summary: The United States restricted nonessential foreign entry at land and ferry crossings from Canada and Mexico from the night of 20–21 March 2020 to reduce COVID-19 transmission. Returning US citizens and permanent residents, trade and other essential journeys remained permitted. Fully vaccinated foreign visitors regained nonessential entry from 8 November 2021, with crossings documented that day; this was conditional reopening for that group.

verification.notes: Inbound nonessential foreign cohort and vaccinated endpoint retained, avoiding all-traffic closure.

summary: Canada restricted ordinary tourist and recreational entry from the United States from 21 March 2020 to contain COVID-19. Citizens and other people with entry rights, essential workers and travellers qualifying for evolving exemptions could still cross. Fully vaccinated US citizens and permanent residents living in and travelling from the United States became eligible for tourist entry on 9 August 2021, followed by broader vaccinated entry in September.

verification.notes: March effective date and August eligible cohort distinguished from earlier quarantine or family exemptions.

summary: French authorities restricted nonessential road passage between Sint Maarten and Saint-Martin from 30 March 2020 during the COVID-19 emergency. Documented cross-border work and urgent medical journeys remained permitted, while shopping, family visits and leisure travel were prohibited. Checks at Bellevue and Quartier d’Orléans were removed around 1–2 June; Dutch controls had ended earlier and barriers on some other roads remained.

verification.notes: Endpoint limited to two French-controlled roads, retaining other barriers and exceptions.

summary: Belize restricted ordinary foreign land arrivals in March 2020 and extended restrictions to returning Belizeans from 5 April, with emergency and other authorised exceptions. Conditional vacation-tourist entry resumed at the northern and western land borders on 31 May 2021. Broader admission and departure for Belizeans and residents was authorised from 7 February 2022; their changing rules and earlier exceptions differed from the tourist reopening.

verification.notes: March tourist onset retained; April tightening and separate tourist/resident endpoints not conflated.

summary: Panamanian truckers blocked freight crossings with Costa Rica from 17 May 2020 during a dispute over Costa Rican COVID-19 rules for foreign drivers. Authorities also imposed separate driver-entry and cargo-routing measures. Some escorted cargo passed before renewed obstruction, and trucks began moving more generally on 26–27 May; the disruption therefore did not stop every truck continuously or end at every crossing simultaneously.

verification.notes: Physical trucker blockades separated from government protocols and limited mid-closure cargo passage.

summary: Nicaraguan authorities halted cargo passage at Peñas Blancas on 18 May 2020 amid a dispute over Costa Rica’s COVID-19 rules for foreign truck drivers, according to Costa Rican officials. Freight movement in both directions was affected. Trucks were documented crossing again on 31 May; the separate Tablillas crossing had a different reopening timetable.

verification.notes: Attributed onset account and transport dispute preserved without adding independent Nicaraguan health motive.

summary: French authorities again restricted nonessential passage from Sint Maarten into Saint-Martin from 31 July 2020 to slow COVID-19 transmission. Work, medical and specified airport-arrival journeys remained exempt. The main checks at Bellevue and Quartier d’Orléans were reported lifted on 16 September, while removal of barriers on other roads followed later.

verification.notes: Main controlled crossings distinguished from later barrier removal; source location conflict checked.

summary: Uruguay tightened its COVID-19 border rules from 21 December 2020, suspending ordinary admission even for citizens and resident foreigners without an applicable exception. Freight, humanitarian and health journeys continued, and later rules admitted some travellers with previously purchased tickets. Normal eligibility for citizens and residents was restored from 1 February 2021; the measure had not stopped every admission or imposed a corresponding general exit ban.

verification.notes: Tightening concerns ordinary resident/citizen eligibility with prebooked and emergency exceptions.

summary: Mexico announced restrictions on nonessential land entry at its southern border from 19 March 2021, citing COVID-19, and renewed them through 21 June. Reporters saw some Guatemalan shoppers turned back at Suchiate, while other travellers negotiated passage and enforcement differed between crossings. The announced end does not establish when enforcement ceased, and equivalent restrictions at the northern border were not demonstrated.

verification.notes: Renewed southern ordered window retained; uneven enforcement and unresolved actual cessation explicit.

summary: The Dominican Republic closed its border with Haiti to people, vehicles and binational markets after President Jovenel Moïse’s assassination on 7 July 2021, citing security and migration concerns. It authorised food exports on 13 July, and food trade resumed at Dajabón on 14 July with controlled admission of Haitian shoppers. This limited commercial reopening did not establish unrestricted passenger access or reopening at every post.

verification.notes: July permission and actual Dajabón trade distinguished; narrow commercial endpoint retained.

summary: US authorities suspended services at the Del Rio port of entry on 17 September 2021 as a large migrant encampment strained resources and raised safety concerns. Traffic was diverted to Eagle Pass. Passenger and pedestrian services were authorised to resume on 25 September and essential passage was reported restored by 27 September; commercial cargo had a separate restart schedule.

verification.notes: Service authorization distinguished from later observed report; no exact first passenger passage asserted.

summary: Protesters opposing pandemic mandates blocked Canada-bound access to the Ambassador Bridge from 7 February 2022, disrupting passenger journeys and trade between Detroit and Windsor. US-bound commercial access was restored by 8 February, while emergency access and alternative crossings remained available. Canada-bound traffic resumed during the night of 13–14 February after the blockade was cleared.

verification.notes: Directional phase preserved; official opening definitions support overnight endpoint range.

summary: A protest blockade obstructed ordinary passenger and commercial access in both directions at the Emerson–Pembina crossing between Manitoba and North Dakota from 10 February 2022. Livestock transport, emergency vehicles, border staff and some local residential traffic continued to pass. The protesters departed and border services resumed on 16 February, ending the disruption at that crossing.

verification.notes: Both-direction ordinary access with documented essential/local exceptions; no impermeability claim.

summary: Canadian authorities suspended traveller and commercial services at Coutts, Alberta, on 12 February 2022 because a protest blockade made access unsafe. Traffic was redirected to other ports. Access and services resumed on 14–15 February; earlier highway protests had allowed intermittent passage and are separate from this shorter service suspension.

verification.notes: February 12 service suspension separated from January intermittent protests; endpoint range retained.

summary: Protesters blocked highway access in both directions at the Pacific Highway crossing between British Columbia and Washington on 12 February 2022, disrupting passenger and commercial traffic. Alternative border crossings remained available. Police reported access restored on 14 February, while the border agency issued its resumption notice on 15 February; a later protest caused a separate interruption.

verification.notes: Police access restoration and agency resumption message retained as range; recurrence not joined.

summary: A renewed protest blocked northbound and southbound access at the Pacific Highway crossing between British Columbia and Washington on 19 February 2022. Passenger and commercial traffic was disrupted, with alternative ports still available. Access reopened that evening, making this a separate interruption of less than a day following the earlier February blockade.

verification.notes: Same-day recurrence separated from earlier multi-day episode and from message timestamp.

summary: Colombia ordered its authorised land and river crossings closed to ordinary travellers from midnight on 12 March until 23:59 on 13 March 2022 for congressional-election security. Colombians living in Venezuela had designated voting access, and exceptional journeys could be permitted. This was an announced period of almost 48 hours; actual reopening at every crossing was not documented.

verification.notes: Used superseding March 12 schedule and exceptions; almost48-hour order not one-day arithmetic.

summary: Colombia ordered ordinary passage at its authorised land and river crossings suspended from 18:00 on 28 May to 06:00 on 30 May 2022 for the presidential election’s first round. Force-majeure and other specified exceptional journeys remained permitted. Pedestrian movement was reported restored at the Cúcuta-area bridges on 30 May, although the evidence does not establish simultaneous reopening across the country.

verification.notes: National 36-hour order and separately observed Cúcuta pedestrian reopening distinguished.

summary: Colombia ordered ordinary passage at its authorised land and river crossings suspended from 18:00 on 18 June to 06:00 on 20 June 2022 for the presidential runoff. Voting-related access and force-majeure journeys were exempt. The evidence establishes a scheduled 36-hour restriction for election security, without confirming enforcement or reopening at every crossing.

verification.notes: Retained ordered rather than observed national window and voting exceptions.

summary: The Dominican Republic closed its frontier with Haiti on 15 September 2023 over a dispute about a canal on the shared river. It permitted controlled food and medicine trade through El Carrizal from 11 October, but Haitian-side restrictions and limited participation delayed actual commerce. Renewed exchange was reported by 20 November; the October permission did not reopen ordinary passenger travel or the entire frontier.

verification.notes: October Dominican permission distinguished from actual commerce and continued Haitian restrictions.

summary: US authorities closed the Lukeville–Sonoyta crossing to pedestrians and vehicles in both directions on 4 December 2023 so staff could be redeployed to process increased migrant arrivals. Other border crossings remained available. The port reopened on 4 January 2024, when local reporting documented commuters returning after a month of disruption.

verification.notes: Both directions and local port scope preserved; actual January field report supports endpoint.

summary: US authorities suspended rail operations at El Paso and Eagle Pass on 18 December 2023 to redeploy border staff for migrant processing. Freight trains in both directions were affected, while road and pedestrian operations followed separate arrangements. The rail crossings reopened on 22 December, although some carriers’ shipment embargoes continued beyond the federal suspension.

verification.notes: Federal crossing closure kept separate from later carrier embargoes and road restrictions.

summary: Venezuela restricted land-frontier passage around its July 2024 presidential election, citing border security. At the Simón Bolívar bridge with Colombia, barriers were reported from the evening of 25 July and ordinary pedestrian and vehicle movement resumed on 29 July. Authorised voter and returnee movements were exceptions, and these observed dates do not establish identical restrictions along the whole frontier or with Brazil.

verification.notes: Local observed bridge interval used despite conflicting national schedule end hours.

summary: Venezuela closed its frontiers with Colombia and Brazil on 10 January 2025 around the presidential inauguration, with officials alleging a security conspiracy. Reopening was announced on the Colombian frontier and confirmed by Brazil’s foreign ministry on 13 January. The sources do not establish identical closing hours, affected traveller categories or exceptions on both frontiers.

verification.notes: Attributed conspiracy allegation and official reopening confirmations; no invented universal traffic scope.

summary: Ecuador restricted foreign passenger entry by land from 8 February 2025 for election security, while exempting Ecuadorians and lawful goods movements. Passage at Aguas Verdes–Huaquillas on the Peruvian frontier resumed on 11 February. A separate municipal obstruction still affected some goods vehicles, and this local reopening does not establish when crossings with Colombia resumed normal operation.

verification.notes: Actual Huaquillas endpoint separated from cargo wall and Colombian frontier.

summary: Ecuador ordered foreign land entry from Colombia and Peru suspended from 16:00 on 11 April until 23:59 on 14 April 2025 for presidential-runoff security. Ecuadorian citizens and lawful trade were exempt. Reporters documented checks at Huaquillas on 12 April, with Ecuadorian travellers and goods still passing; the scheduled expiry does not confirm when ordinary foreign entry actually resumed.

verification.notes: Ordered inclusive expiry and single implementation observation distinguished; inbound cohort preserved.

summary: Colombia ordered ordinary traveller entry and exit at authorised land and river crossings suspended from 18:00 on 7 March to 06:00 on 9 March 2026 for election security. Exceptional journeys could be authorised. Reporting confirmed reopening after 36 hours at the bridges linking Norte de Santander and Táchira, but the same operation was not independently documented at every Colombian crossing.

verification.notes: National ordered window separated from actual local bridge-group reopening.

summary: Colombia ordered its authorised land and river crossings closed to ordinary travellers from 18:00 on 30 May to 06:00 on 1 June 2026 for election security, allowing specified exceptional journeys. Rumichaca, on the Ecuadorian border, was reported reopened after the 36-hour interruption. That local account does not establish identical enforcement or reopening at all national border posts.

verification.notes: Rumichaca actual reopening distinguished from nationwide scheduled order.

summary: Colombia ordered ordinary traveller entry and exit at authorised land and river crossings suspended over 20–22 June 2026 for election security, retaining humanitarian and other exceptional passage. The amended order intended an earlier start than previously announced, but its exact enforceable starting hour is uncertain. Reopening on 22 June was reported at crossings with Venezuela in Norte de Santander, Arauca and La Guajira.

verification.notes: Superseded schedule not reused; no exact48-hour enforcement or all-cargo closure asserted.

summary: Colombia ordered its authorised land and river posts closed from 18:00 on 8 March to 16:00 on 11 March 2018 for congressional-election security, except for force-majeure journeys. At Rumichaca, the measure stopped pedestrians and vehicles, including buses and freight, in both directions. Passage there resumed shortly after 16:00 on 11 March; this local observation does not confirm operation at every Colombian post.

verification.notes: National order and observed Rumichaca event distinguished; passenger/freight and two directions supported.

summary: Colombia scheduled border closures for its May 2018 presidential election, with a longer restriction on the Venezuelan frontier. Authorised crossings with Venezuela were to close from midnight on 24 May to midnight on 28 May, while other land and river crossings were covered from midnight on 26 May to 16:00 on 27 May. Exceptional journeys were permitted; the schedules do not establish actual reopening at every post.

verification.notes: Separate Venezuela96-hour and other40-hour schedules retained as orders.

summary: Colombia scheduled closures at authorised land and river crossings for the June 2018 presidential runoff, allowing force-majeure journeys. The Venezuelan frontier was covered from midnight on 14 June to midnight on 18 June, while other frontiers were covered from midnight on 16 June to 16:00 on 17 June. These were announced election-security windows; uninterrupted enforcement and completed reopening at every post were not established.

verification.notes: Two frontier schedules and ordered nature preserved.

summary: A Brazilian court order temporarily suspended formal admission of Venezuelan migrants at Pacaraima from the afternoon of 6 August until the morning of 7 August 2018. Brazilians, other nationalities and Venezuelans leaving Brazil could still cross. Federal police reported lifting the restriction after an appellate decision; this was an overnight migration restriction of less than 24 hours, not a general halt to border movement.

verification.notes: Targeted migrant admission, exempt directions/nationalities and under24-hour duration retained; avoided conflicting court attribution.

summary: US authorities briefly suspended northbound vehicles and PedEast pedestrian processing at San Ysidro on 19 November 2018 while installing emergency security measures against a possible migrant rush. No such rush materialised, according to the border agency. Pedestrian processing and selected vehicle lanes resumed after about three hours, while PedWest and southbound vehicles remained unaffected; some vehicle lanes stayed closed longer.

verification.notes: Initial partial service restoration distinguished from remaining closed lanes and later incidents.

summary: US authorities stopped pedestrian and vehicle passage in both directions at San Ysidro during a confrontation with migrants on 25 November 2018, citing security and attempted unlawful entry. Pedestrians and vehicles were readmitted in stages later that afternoon, while Otay Mesa remained open. Five lanes already closed for earlier security work were separate from this incident’s reopening.

verification.notes: Same-day staged reopening and earlier lane closures kept distinct.

summary: Colombia suspended ordinary boat-departure authorisations at specified international river ports for its October 2019 regional elections. Restrictions began on 24 October along the Venezuelan frontier and on 26 October at the designated Amazonian ports, with both scheduled to end at 16:00 on 27 October. Humanitarian, exceptional and certain previously authorised customs-transit journeys could proceed; actual restart at every river port was not documented.

verification.notes: River departure authorization only; no extrapolation to land routes or general freight exemption.

summary: Colombia ordered twelve land and river migration posts with Venezuela, Brazil, Peru and Ecuador closed from midnight on 20 November to 05:00 on 22 November 2019 before a national strike. Authorities said the measure would support orderly, peaceful demonstrations, and exceptional journeys could be authorised. Reporting confirmed disruption at Rumichaca, but did not establish when all affected posts actually reopened.

verification.notes: Attributed public-order rationale and local observation separated from national53-hour order.

summary: PedWest at San Ysidro suspended ordinary pedestrian service on 5 April 2020 after pandemic-related traffic declined, while the nearby PedEast crossing remained available. The facility briefly handled Ukrainian refugees in 2022 but did not restore ordinary northbound service until 9 January 2023. That reopening offered limited morning and early-afternoon hours, rather than full two-way or round-the-clock service.

verification.notes: Facility-specific suspension continues beyond national ban; exceptional refugee processing and limited endpoint retained.

summary: US authorities suspended ordinary northbound pedestrian service at PedWest on 14 September 2023 to redeploy staff for migrant processing. CBP One appointments continued, and travellers could use PedEast or Otay Mesa. Ordinary northbound service resumed on 16 November with hours from 06:00 to 14:00; southbound service, already unavailable before this suspension, was not restored then.

verification.notes: Appointments and alternatives preserved; northbound ordinary service only.

summary: US authorities suspended northbound vehicle processing at Eagle Pass International Bridge I on 20 September 2023 to reassign staff to migrant processing. Pedestrians could still cross and vehicles could use Bridge II. Bridge I reopened to vehicles on 16 October; the evidence does not establish an equivalent southbound suspension, and rail operations had separate dates.

verification.notes: Supported northbound direction retained; rail and Bridge II not included.

summary: US authorities suspended the Eagle Pass international railway crossing on 20 September 2023 to redeploy border staff for migrant processing. Union Pacific reported freight trains held on both sides of the border, while its other international gateways remained open. The railway interchange reopened at midnight on 23 September; separate carrier embargoes did not share the crossing’s exact suspension dates.

verification.notes: Both train directions and actual carrier reopening retained, separate embargoes excluded.

summary: US authorities suspended northbound passenger vehicles at Eagle Pass Bridge I from the afternoon of 27 November 2023 to redeploy staff amid increased migrant arrivals. Southbound vehicles and pedestrians remained able to use Bridge I, and cargo continued through Bridge II. Northbound passenger service resumed on 4 January 2024; truck queues and additional inspections elsewhere were separate disruptions.

verification.notes: Northbound vehicles only, with southbound/pedestrian exceptions and continuing cargo.

summary: US authorities again suspended ordinary pedestrian service at PedWest from 9 December 2023 to reassign officers to migrant processing. Travellers used PedEast during the interruption. PedWest reopened on 4 January 2024 with separate daily hours for northbound and southbound pedestrians, rather than round-the-clock service; other border closures reported alongside it had different scopes and dates.

verification.notes: December recurrence and limited direction-specific reopening preserved.

summary: Protesters obstructed La Amistad bridge at El Amatillo on 22 December 2017 during Honduras’s disputed-election crisis, disrupting entry from El Salvador into Honduras. Police used tear gas to disperse the demonstrators. The report did not confirm unrestricted passage afterwards, so the start, duration and completed reopening remain uncertain; it does not establish a closure lasting a full day.

verification.notes: Dated observation and unresolved post-dispersal passage retained; reverse direction not inferred.

summary: Parents and teachers blocked access serving the Suchiate crossings between Mexico and Guatemala from 19 March 2019, demanding reconstruction of earthquake-damaged schools. Freight at Suchiate II was disrupted, with trucks stranded on both sides despite Guatemalan customs remaining operational. The blockade was lifted and traffic resumed on 21 March after an agreement; the same continuous impact at Suchiate I was not established.

verification.notes: School-reconstruction protest onset separated from holiday and earlier protest; Suchiate II endpoint supported.

summary: Truckers blocked freight access at Peñas Blancas on 19 March 2019 in protest against Nicaragua’s new US$50 temporary vehicle-registration fee. Nicaraguan trucks seeking to enter Costa Rica were among those affected. The obstructing truck was moved that afternoon in the presence of traffic police; this was a same-day protest blockade, not a Costa Rican government border closure.

verification.notes: Actor corrected to truckers, fee start not mistaken for blockade start, same-day clearing retained.

summary: Political unrest in Bolivia prevented the Desaguadero/Puerto Acosta customs administration from operating from 12 to 23 November 2019, while roadblocks disrupted traffic along the Peruvian frontier. Some travellers could still cross on foot. Passenger and truck movement at Desaguadero resumed on 24 November during a temporary truce, but the exact restoration of customs services and conditions at Puerto Acosta remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Customs nonoperation separated from physical traffic and temporary truce; pedestrian exceptions preserved.

summary: Mexican authorities temporarily stopped a migrant caravan at the Rodolfo Robles bridge from Guatemala on 18 January 2020 after a confrontation at the gate. Officials described the action as maintaining order and requiring registration. Small groups were admitted for processing later the same day, ending the immediate stoppage without establishing unrestricted entry or a broader closure to all border traffic.

verification.notes: Same-day selective processing retained, not unrestricted reopening or later caravan episode.

summary: Transporters blocked international freight at Peñas Blancas in October 2020, demanding changes to GPS monitoring, permitted stays and reciprocal treatment for regional trucks. The blockage was documented by 8 October, and normal cargo movement was reported restored on 9 October. The exact start remains uncertain; border offices stayed staffed, and the evidence does not establish the effect on passengers.

verification.notes: Imprecise October onset not asserted as October1; freight-only impact and actual later restoration retained.

summary: Truckers blocked international freight at Paso Canoas from the evening of 21 October 2020 in a dispute over Panama’s treatment of Costa Rican trucks and requirements to transfer or reassign loads. An agreement was reached on 23 October, but cargo movements restarted the following morning after customs reopened. Passenger impacts and the precise effects in each direction were not established.

verification.notes: Agreement date not mistaken for actual cargo return; distinct triggering direction retained.

summary: Protesters renewed blockades at Desaguadero on 4 January 2023 during Peru’s political crisis, disrupting the road connection with Bolivia. Humanitarian movements later allowed some stranded trucks to return, and negotiated arrangements in March opened passenger and freight access on different days of the week. These intermittent openings and differing rules mean the disruption cannot be described as one uninterrupted January-to-March closure.

verification.notes: Renewed January observation, humanitarian return and recurring March access preserved without aggregate duration.

summary: Migrants stranded between Chile and Peru blocked the road linking Chacalluta and Santa Rosa on the morning of 25 April 2023, protesting their inability to enter Peru without the required documents. Vehicles and passengers travelling between the countries were affected. Police cleared the road that morning; the brief blockade was separate from the migrants’ longer wait and other April incidents.

verification.notes: Under24-hour actual road blockage distinguished from longer inadmissibility and separate April16 event.

summary: Stranded migrants blocked the road between Santa Rosa and Chacalluta on 29 April 2023 while seeking entry into Peru and onward travel home. The initial two-way blockage lasted more than six hours before afternoon clearance. A later blockade ended with traffic from Arica to Tacna restored, but the opposite direction remained obstructed at the last report, leaving its eventual reopening uncertain.

verification.notes: Separated morning clearance from recurrence and directional partial restoration; no all-day continuity.

summary: Protest groups and truckers repeatedly obstructed Paso Canoas in September–October 2020 over fiscal proposals and unequal treatment of regional transporters. Traffic resumed on 4 October before barriers were rebuilt that night, and further negotiations and changes of protest groups followed. Barriers were removed on 14 October and freight moved again on 15 October, with priority for humanitarian and perishable cargo; the episode was not one continuous fifteen-day closure.

verification.notes: Interrupted chronology and changing actors preserved; no aggregate continuous duration.

summary: Guyana restricted ordinary travel at Lethem–Bonfim during March 2020 in response to COVID-19, while allowing specified goods deliveries and limited shopping exchanges on Thursdays. Personal travel on Fridays was added from 1 October 2021 under health conditions, followed by permission for weekday opening in November. The first Guyanese restriction date is uncertain, and these selective arrangements did not stop all movement across the Brazilian frontier.

verification.notes: Bounded March onset not borrowed from Brazil; October partial easing and later November permission separated.

summary: Venezuela stopped cars, trucks and pedestrians at the Pacaraima–Santa Elena de Uairén crossing on 22 January 2025 during military exercises. Contemporary reports disagree on whether passage resumed that evening or on 23 January. The evidence therefore does not resolve whether the interruption exceeded 24 hours, and it is separate from the earlier inauguration-related closure.

verification.notes: Contemporaneous endpoint conflict preserved without inventing recurrence or duration.

summary: Indigenous communities blocked vehicle passage at Rumichaca between Colombia and Ecuador from 26 February 2025 after Ecuadorian forces demolished local pedestrian bridges. Protesters objected to lost community connections and effects on their rights; Ecuador had cited illicit use of the demolished bridges. Vehicles resumed crossing on the night of 28 February following negotiations, while intermittent humanitarian pedestrian passage had continued during the blockade.

verification.notes: Vehicle scope, humanitarian windows and contrasting attributed explanations retained; negotiation time not reopening clock.

summary: Ecuador restricted secondary land crossings from 24 December 2025, citing organised crime and illicit arms movements, while keeping Rumichaca and Huaquillas authorised. Reopening was staggered: pedestrian access returned before ordinary vehicles at Macará on 7 July 2026 and Lalamor–Zapotillo on 8 July. San Miguel was still restricted on 9 July, and La Balsa and Jimbura on 17 July; local, oil-transport and special-permit exceptions varied, and those July reports do not establish later status.

verification.notes: Separate crossing/traffic endpoints retained and later unknown status explicit; no same endpoint assigned nationwide.

summary: Salvadoran public-sector unionists obstructed customs operations at La Hachadura on 19 March 2019, affecting traffic from Guatemala, including freight. The precise legislative grievance and the blockade’s first and last dates remain uncertain. Later reporting confirms some trucks were processed in May, but that followed a separate customs-system disruption and does not show that the March protest continued until then.

verification.notes: Single March observation separated from May IT disruption and later partial processing; grievance not invented.

summary: Truckers blocked freight entry and exit at Peñas Blancas on the morning of 30 April 2020 after Costa Rica reduced their permitted commercial stay to 72 hours. Perishable and urgent cargo was among the traffic affected. Police reported the obstruction removed and normal truck movement restored around 05:00 on 1 May; passenger effects and an exact elapsed duration were not established.

verification.notes: Trucker protest over pandemic transport rule, not state cargo closure; overnight duration kept uncertain.

summary: Traders at Bonfim blocked supply trucks heading from Brazil to Lethem in September 2021, protesting unequal access under Guyana’s pandemic travel rules. A six-hour action on 9 September was followed by a renewed blockade from 15 September that persisted later that month. Protests had ended by 2 October after personal-travel rules eased, but the exact freight reopening date is unknown and alternative supply routes remained available.

verification.notes: Two separate protest phases retained and ended-by observation not converted into exact reopening.

summary: Migrants blocked Peru-bound vehicle lanes between Chacalluta and Santa Rosa on 22 June 2023 after being refused entry into Peru without the required documents. Chilean police restored traffic after a short protest, reported locally as almost twenty minutes. The migrants remained beside the road afterwards, so the reopening of vehicle traffic did not resolve their separate admission restrictions.

verification.notes: Short June22 event separate from April crisis and June23 publication date; approximate minutes attributed.

summary: International passenger-service drivers blocked vehicle access at Santa Rosa on 29 November 2023, demanding round-the-clock operation at the Peru–Chile crossing. Some vehicles passed intermittently and pedestrians could walk past the obstruction. One report documented clearance and normal traffic near midday after talks, while later accounts left the final situation uncertain; the evidence does not support an uninterrupted full-day closure.

verification.notes: Intermittent access and reported midday clearance retained; later accounts not turned into invented recurrence.

summary: Venezuelan-side controls stopped ordinary traffic at Santa Elena de Uairén–Pacaraima on 3 January 2026 following a reported US attack. Brazilian tourists were allowed to return before wider movement resumed later the same day. Accounts differ on the hours of closure and reopening, and no official Venezuelan order was recovered to establish the precise reason or a uniform restriction on every traveller.

verification.notes: Same-day staged reopening preserved; security motive not asserted as official fact.

summary: Traders and transporters began intermittently blocking vehicles at Rumichaca on 9 March 2026 in protest against the Colombia–Ecuador tariff dispute and its effects on livelihoods. Freight trucks, cars and passenger vehicles were affected, while pedestrians and motorcycles could pass during documented stages. Traffic resumed gradually on 27 March; the intervening openings mean the protest period was not continuously closed for its full length.

verification.notes: Intermittent regime and documented passenger exceptions retained; no summed closed hours.

summary: Colombian teachers occupied Rumichaca bridge on 23 May 2017 during a labour protest over pay and working conditions. International passenger vehicles and freight were blocked, with trucks queuing on the Ecuadorian side, while pedestrians could cross. The occupation ended after about three hours before the march continued into Ipiales; an exact moment of full traffic normalisation was not recorded.

verification.notes: Event body date overrides dynamic metadata; same-day vehicle occupation and pedestrian exception retained.

summary: Protesters blocked Canadian-side vehicle access to Rainbow Bridge on 16 February 2020 in solidarity with Wet’suwet’en opposition to pipeline development. The action disrupted cross-border road traffic for several hours before demonstrators left voluntarily that day. The evidence does not establish the exact reopening time, the effect on pedestrians or identical restrictions in both directions.

verification.notes: Rainbow Bridge identity prioritized over inconsistent paragraph; voluntary departure not exact official reopening.

summary: Pipeline-solidarity protesters disrupted the Thousand Islands crossing on 17 February 2020, prompting temporary restrictions at the customs entry points and on northbound highway access. Cross-border vehicles were affected, while local access to Wellesley Island reportedly remained possible. The crossing reopened by about 15:00 that day; differing times for the protest, approach restrictions and port suspension prevent a precise elapsed duration.

verification.notes: Port/approach milestones separated, local island access retained, same-day ending supported.

summary: Haiti restricted passenger traffic at its four principal crossings with the Dominican Republic on 16–17 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission. Freight with reduced crews and voluntary Haitian returns continued under exceptions. Haiti authorised reopening on 30 June, but Dominican restrictions remained in force, so the Haitian decision did not establish restored ordinary passage on both sides of the frontier.

verification.notes: Haitian formal permission separate from actual exempt movement and continuing Dominican restrictions.

summary: The Dominican Republic restricted ordinary passenger movement and suspended border markets from 19 March 2020 to prevent COVID-19 transmission. Goods and Haitians returning to Haiti could still pass. Haitian customers were readmitted to the Dajabón market in a limited pilot on 6 November, capped at fifty entries per hour; this did not constitute general reopening of all Dominican border crossings.

verification.notes: National restriction and specifically limited Dajabón market endpoint separated.

summary: US authorities temporarily stopped northbound vehicles and pedestrian passage at Paso del Norte on 12 March 2023 after a large group of migrants approached the crossing. The border agency said the barriers were intended to prevent a mass entry and protect ordinary trade and travel. Pedestrian processing and one vehicle lane resumed that evening; the evidence does not establish when every lane reopened.

verification.notes: Sub-day emergency suspension to first partial reopening, not final all-lane normalisation.

summary: Migrants repeatedly obstructed the Chilean road approach between Chacalluta and Santa Rosa on 28 November 2025, initially blocking vehicles toward Peru and later affecting both directions. Some passengers walked across and negotiated pauses allowed vehicles through. Road clearance was reported by midday, and normal flows the next day, but the final end of all intermittent obstruction was not precisely established.

verification.notes: Recurring vehicle action distinct from admission rules; later-published morning footage not invented recurrence.

summary: Mototaxi operators blocked vehicles at the Paraguayan end of the Posadas–Encarnación bridge on 13 June 2017, opposing tighter Argentine transport checks and motorcycle seizures after a fatal collision. Traffic was restored that evening. Reports differ on the precise hours, and the evidence does not establish pedestrian effects or a continuous link with an earlier protest the previous day.

verification.notes: Tuesday action and actual evening restoration separated from Monday action and inconsistent clocks.

summary: Cross-border porters and traders blocked vehicles on the Bermejo–Aguas Blancas bridge on 5 April 2019 in protest against changes to Argentina’s small-importer rules. The restrictions affected road traffic entering and leaving across the Bolivia–Argentina frontier. Protesters lifted the blockade late that afternoon for negotiations; this was a temporary pause, rather than confirmation of a final settlement.

verification.notes: Initial bridge blockade ends at negotiating pause; separate high-water outage excluded.

summary: Truck drivers deliberately obstructed La Hachadura–Pedro de Alvarado on the night of 7 May 2019 after delays caused by a new customs declaration system. Freight from Guatemala into El Salvador was affected. Accounts of clearance and renewed obstruction the next day conflict; later official reporting confirms freight processing by 19 May, but does not establish the first reopening or a continuous blockade throughout that period.

verification.notes: Intentional blockade separated from preceding technical delays; later processing is bound only.

summary: Truck drivers blocked the El Jobo/Las Chinamas–Valle Nuevo crossing on 8 May 2019 while seeking Guatemalan exit paperwork needed to enter El Salvador. A driver was documented entering El Salvador the following morning, confirming that some freight access had resumed by 9 May. The exact clearance time, effects on pedestrians and other lanes, and whether the blockage exceeded 24 hours remain uncertain.

verification.notes: Direction and paperwork grievance supported; first observed later truck not exact reopening.

summary: Venezuela restricted vehicles at Santa Elena–Pacaraima on 18–19 May 2018 for presidential-election security, with pedestrian restrictions following during 19 May. People and vehicles were reported able to use the official crossing again on 21 May. Informal routes remained usable, and the evidence concerns this Venezuelan-side restriction rather than a closure of every Brazil–Venezuela crossing.

verification.notes: Distinct vehicle/pedestrian onset, overlapping phases and informal access preserved.

summary: Anti-migrant protesters obstructed the BR-174 approach at Pacaraima on 18 August 2018 during violence against Venezuelans following an alleged robbery. Some Venezuelans nevertheless crossed back into Venezuela during the unrest. Normal border operation was reported by the next morning, but conflicting accounts of direction and affected travellers prevent treating the episode as a continuous two-way closure.

verification.notes: Alleged trigger attributed; migrant departures and disputed direction preclude total closure interpretation.

summary: Residents blocked vehicles at Amatal bridge on the Guatemalan approach to San Cristóbal customs from 4 November 2019 to demand road repairs. Freight, including perishable goods, and other road users were affected, while pedestrians could pass and alternative routes remained available. Police confirmed clearance on 8 November; the protest obstructed access rather than suspending customs’ legal authority or closing every frontier route.

verification.notes: Deliberate road-access blockade and pedestrian alternatives retained; not roadworks or legal customs closure.

summary: Mexican police barricaded the Rodolfo Robles bridge gate on 19 October 2018 during a confrontation with migrant-caravan participants seeking entry from Guatemala without documents. Some asylum applicants had entered earlier, and selected groups of children and adults were admitted after the afternoon stoppage. This was a brief, selective interruption, not a continuous ban on all people crossing the frontier.

verification.notes: Initial sub-day gate stoppage separated from morning admissions, river crossings and later vehicle restriction.

summary: Motorists approaching Chile at Pino Hachado were reportedly turned back on 24 May 2017 during a customs strike, with Icalma also described as affected. Other reports said regional crossings remained open and the union maintained emergency shifts. Later operation at Pino Hachado is confirmed, but conflicting accounts and a separate snow interruption leave the strike-related closure’s duration and reopening uncertain.

verification.notes: Specific reported turnbacks retained alongside contradictory opening reports; no continuous May-to-June claim.

summary: Guatemalan truckers repeatedly blocked cargo entry into Belize at Melchor de Mencos–Western Border from 31 August 2021, objecting to repeated COVID-19 tests and escort or taxi charges. Trucks carrying various goods were affected. Freight resumed on 2 September after the disputed charges were removed, while testing remained; passenger effects and uninterrupted closure between the repeated blockages were not established.

verification.notes: Intermittent cargo protest and fees/testing distinction preserved.

summary: Truckers blocked freight at Las Manos on the Honduras–Nicaragua border in October 2023 over reciprocal visa requirements for drivers. An initial action on 11–12 October cleared on 12 October, followed by renewed intermittent obstruction from 18–19 October. Cargo operations resumed on the night of 24 October after an agreement; buses, light vehicles and some perishable loads were allowed during documented stages.

verification.notes: Two actions and intermittent access retained; Guasaule endpoint not substituted.

summary: Opposition protesters seized the Agua Caliente crossing on 30 November 2017 during Honduras’s disputed-election crisis, disrupting commercial movement at the Guatemalan frontier. Later reports described violence, blockades and reduced customs hours in the area. They do not establish that this particular blockade continued without interruption, and its exact duration, passenger effects and reopening remain uncertain.

verification.notes: November30 observation not December1 publication onset; later reduced hours not continuous blockade evidence.

summary: Honduran authorities closed the Agua Caliente checkpoint on 20 October 2018 following migrant-caravan confrontations, citing safety and control of departures. Pre-authorised freight drivers arriving from Guatemala were readmitted by 23 October, and documented Honduran departures resumed on 24 October. Separate Guatemalan customs restrictions and conflicting reports prevent treating these steps as a single unrestricted bilateral reopening.

verification.notes: Honduran onset and separate freight/national-departure restoration preserved; Guatemala timeline unresolved.

summary: Farmers blocked commercial traffic at several Ciudad Juárez-area crossings from 24 November 2025 in protests over agricultural livelihoods and water legislation. Cargo disruption affected the Bridge of the Americas, Zaragoza–Ysleta and San Jerónimo–Santa Teresa, with Guadalupe–Tornillo also blocked by 25 November. Commercial operations were reported normal by 28 November; interruptions varied, and ordinary cars were explicitly permitted at the Bridge of the Americas.

verification.notes: Four crossings and later Tornillo observation retained without common onset or continuous duration.

summary: Renewed protests over water legislation disrupted cargo at several Chihuahua–US crossings from 3 December 2025, with closures and partial openings varying by crossing and direction. US border bulletins confirmed normal cargo processing at the Bridge of the Americas, Ysleta, Santa Teresa, Tornillo and Columbus by 5 December. A separate interruption at Presidio–Ojinaga also ended that day, although its precise onset and motive were not established; passenger restrictions were not demonstrated.

verification.notes: Port-specific and direction-changing cargo events preserved; Presidio motive not borrowed from others.

summary: Protesters blocked commercial cargo at Agua Prieta–Douglas from 3 December 2025 in opposition to water legislation. Private vehicles and pedestrians continued crossing, and nearby Naco was unaffected. The blockade was reported lifted on the afternoon of 4 December, but the evidence does not establish whether freight passage resumed between the two days or which directions were continuously blocked.

verification.notes: Cargo-only scope and overnight continuity uncertainty retained; later CBP confirmation not reopening date.

summary: Protests against higher petrol prices obstructed El Chaparral in January 2017, prompting US authorities to divert southbound vehicles approaching San Ysidro. Separate interruptions on 7 and 8 January lasted roughly four and two hours before vehicle access was restored. Southbound pedestrians and all northbound users could still cross, so these were selective, brief disruptions rather than a two-day closure of the port.

verification.notes: Two same-day diversions, directions and exempt pedestrians preserved.

summary: Agricultural protesters intermittently blocked commercial vehicles at Nogales–Mariposa from 24 to 26 November 2025, citing support for farming and insecurity. Private cars and pedestrians continued to cross, and some trucks were released between renewed obstructions. Cargo access was restored on 26 November, but changing locations, directions and opening windows prevent treating the whole period as continuously closed.

verification.notes: Intermittent releases and shifting cargo scope retained; no continuous two-day duration.

summary: Protesters opposed to water legislation obstructed the Mexicali–Calexico east commercial crossing from 4 December 2025, blocking northbound freight and trapping trucks inside Mexican export customs. Partial access returned on 8 December, followed by reported import and export movement that afternoon. The initial southbound impact and precise reopening times remain uncertain; a protest camp staying nearby did not mean the cargo blockade continued.

verification.notes: Contemporary Dec4 onset preferred; trapped-truck release overlaps main reopening and is not another closure.

summary: Anti-mandate protests caused separate US-bound disruptions at two Canada–US crossings in February 2022. Highway access to Blue Water Bridge at Sarnia was blocked on 6 February and reopened that day after nearly nine hours. Commercial passage at Peace Bridge was suspended from the afternoon of 13 February until reopening by the following morning; later highway diversions did not amount to an additional port closure.

verification.notes: Distinct bridges and episodes, final inquiry timing and functioning later diversion preserved.

summary: Truckers blocked freight in both directions at the Melchor–Benque bridge between Guatemala and Belize from 11 May 2020, opposing a requirement to substitute drivers under pandemic transport arrangements. Cargo purchases and deliveries resumed on the afternoon of 13 May. The action interrupted trade for more than a day, while the separate COVID-19 restrictions governing passengers followed their own rules.

verification.notes: Both cargo directions and actual Wednesday restoration supported; passenger rules not conflated.

summary: Cargo processing on the Mexican side of the Santa Elena crossing was disrupted from about 18 March 2026, delaying imports into Belize. Deliveries resumed on 24 March, while Corozal Free Zone operations and visitor access were reported unaffected. News accounts attributed the disruption to extortion, but Belize’s ambassador said the alleged threats and responsible actors had not been officially confirmed by Mexican authorities.

verification.notes: Extortion allegation expressly attributed, scope limited to inbound cargo, notification time not exact onset.

summary: Brazil restricted nonexempt foreign land entry from Uruguay from 22 March 2020 to limit COVID-19 transmission. Citizens, qualifying family members and residents, freight, authorised humanitarian travel and documented border residents remained exempt. The restriction was renewed in April and later replaced by other rules; broader conditional land admission was permitted by 9 December 2021, without establishing the first relaxation at every crossing.

verification.notes: Separate Uruguay order and renewal distinguished from eight-neighbour order and December later bound.

summary: A group of Nicaraguans returning from Panama through Costa Rica was refused entry at Peñas Blancas on the evening of 26 June 2020 and admitted the following day. Reports differ on the number of returnees and hours spent waiting, but describe an overnight interruption of less than 24 hours. No official explanation was established, and the episode does not demonstrate a border-wide closure.

verification.notes: No health rationale inferred from pandemic context; group-specific overnight denial only.

summary: Protests demanding senior prosecutors’ resignations disrupted named Guatemala–Mexico crossings in October 2023 amid disputes over the electoral process. Reports identified obstruction at El Ceibo and Tecún Umán on 7 October, and customs-related disruption at El Carmen and La Mesilla on 9 October. Road access changed during later protests, but the exact closure and reopening dates for each customs post, and the full effects on passengers and freight, remain unresolved.

verification.notes: Separate dated post/customs observations not extended using later road bulletins.

summary: Customs operations at Agua Caliente, between Guatemala and Honduras, were suspended from 20 September 2021 for Bailey-bridge installation, with heavy freight diverted through Corinto. Restoration was announced for noon on 9 December, and same-day reporting described services resuming for light and heavy vehicles. The evidence supports the customs suspension and reported restoration, without establishing uninterrupted denial of every type of crossing.

verification.notes: Works-related formal suspension and service report retained; Corinto extended hours not endpoint.

summary: Guatemalan authorities announced a complete entry and exit suspension at Agua Caliente–Nueva Ocotepeque from 18:00 on 24 May to 06:00 on 26 May 2025 for paving at the Bailey-bridge entrance. Travellers were advised to use alternative crossings. The sources describe a planned 36-hour closure, including the possibility of earlier completion, but do not confirm actual enforcement or reopening.

verification.notes: Future maintenance notices not converted into observed closure or expiry reopening.

summary: Truckers deliberately obstructed freight on the Argentine approach to Cristo Redentor in January 2022, protesting delays caused by Chilean COVID-19 testing requirements. Chile-bound freight was blocked from 17 January, with a separate obstruction of trucks entering Argentina from 20 January; both were still reported affected on 26 January. Later reports describe settlement and clearance, but do not establish the first restored passage in each direction.

verification.notes: Physical protest distinguished from queues, tourist rules and threatened staff action; directional starts retained.

summary: Residents blocked the Yacuiba–Salvador Mazza international bridge on the morning of 29 May 2023 to demand completion of a sewer project. Following a midday agreement, passenger buses and small vehicles were reported crossing again. The action ended within the day despite an announced 24-hour protest, and the evidence does not establish a universal pedestrian ban or the exact time all traffic resumed.

verification.notes: Actual same-day passage supersedes planned24-hour protest; returning cohort limited to documented vehicles.

summary: Cross-border porters blocked the Yacuiba–Salvador Mazza bridge from 3 July 2023, protesting customs treatment and seizures affecting their trade. The blockade disrupted international freight and was still active on 4 July. A report published on 6 July confirmed lifting and trucks moving in both directions, but did not identify the exact reopening day or establish continuous exclusion of every passenger.

verification.notes: July4–6 ending uncertainty retained without exact72-hour claim.

summary: Health workers blocked the Yacuiba–Salvador Mazza bridge from 22 July 2024, disrupting international buses, freight and other vehicles. Negotiated pauses allowed some traffic through, including buses and light vehicles travelling toward Argentina on the first day. Police cleared the blockade on 28 July and vehicles returned; the intervening exceptions mean the full period cannot be counted as uninterrupted closure.

verification.notes: Contemporary July22 onset preferred over conflicting retrospective dates; actual negotiated passage retained.

summary: Civic protesters blocked freight access at Yacuiba–Salvador Mazza from 31 May 2021, demanding employment, economic recovery measures and vaccination. Organisers said ambulances and oxygen trucks would be allowed through. Lifting was reported on the evening of 1 June and cleared freight access confirmed by 2 June; continuing pandemic restrictions on ordinary passengers were a separate measure.

verification.notes: Reported lifting and corroborated later access distinguished; announced emergency exemptions not claimed as logged passage.

summary: Cross-border porters blocked freight at Yacuiba–Salvador Mazza from 17 July 2017, demanding comparable customs treatment and protection of their livelihoods. Negotiations allowed some perishable loads through in both directions before the blockade resumed. Lifting and renewed truck passage were reported on 25–26 July, leaving the exact operational endpoint uncertain and ruling out an uninterrupted ban on all freight throughout the period.

verification.notes: Intermittent negotiated freight exceptions and bounded endpoint retained.

summary: Truckers blocked commercial lanes at Pharr–Reynosa and Ysleta–Zaragoza from 11 April 2022 in protest against additional Texas inspections and resulting delays. Freight was affected in both directions, while personal vehicles and pedestrians at Ysleta were reported unaffected. The Ysleta protest was removed late on 12 April and commercial operations at both facilities were reported restored by 13 April; the inspections and their queues continued separately.

verification.notes: Two overlapping port episodes not summed; continuing inspections distinguished from protest blockage.

summary: US authorities suspended commercial cargo services at El Paso’s Bridge of the Americas from 14 April 2023 to redeploy officers for migrant processing. Cargo inspections resumed on the morning of 18 April. The notice concerned that cargo facility, not passenger services or every nearby crossing, and the period included normal nonoperating hours rather than four full lost working days.

verification.notes: Cargo-service formal interval and actual morning reopening retained; routine closed hours not additional closure.

summary: Northbound circulation at Pharr–Reynosa was interrupted during a farmers’ protest on 29 May 2024 over agricultural prices and support. Passage was restored later that day, but reports differ on whether protesters directly obstructed traffic or officials closed the gates during the demonstration. They also disagree on the number of hours, so the evidence supports a brief same-day disruption without a precise duration.

verification.notes: Mechanism and duration disagreements preserved; unofficial security conjecture omitted.

summary: Farmers obstructed access to Pharr–Reynosa in July 2025, demanding compensation for low sorghum prices and unpaid support. US-bound freight was blocked on 7–8 July, with withdrawal reported on 9 July. A separate action on 11 July affected freight and private vehicles before commercial traffic resumed that afternoon; uncertain temporary openings and mixed reporting prevent combining the actions into one continuous closure.

verification.notes: July7–9 and July11 actions separated; composite highway exceptions not transferred to bridge.

summary: Pipeline-solidarity protesters occupied an island road and the Cornwall bridge approach in the Seaway International Bridge system on 7 February 2020. Non-emergency traffic from both countries was restricted, while emergency passage remained possible. Traffic resumed around 16:30 after approximately two hours of operating restrictions; the obstruction was on the Cornwall Island approach, rather than directly on the international boundary.

verification.notes: Physical approach location, both directions and emergency-only access preserved; council sponsorship not inferred.

summary: Colombia ordered ordinary passage at authorised land and river border posts suspended from 18:00 on 28 October to 16:00 on 29 October 2023 for territorial-election security. Local notices named Rumichaca, Mataje and San Miguel, with force-majeure and emergency exceptions. This was a scheduled 22-hour restriction, not a documented closure exceeding one day, and actual reopening was not confirmed.

verification.notes: 22-hour order distinguished from alcohol ban and one-date arithmetic.

summary: Venezuela restricted ordinary pedestrian and vehicle passage at San Antonio’s access to the Simón Bolívar bridge from 23 May 2025 around the 25 May elections. A humanitarian corridor remained available. Barriers were removed and ordinary traffic resumed on the morning of 27 May, after the announced restriction expired; this local account does not establish the same timetable or cargo conditions at every frontier crossing.

verification.notes: Observed local endpoint distinguished from legal expiry without inferred extension; humanitarian exception retained.

summary: Venezuelan authorities restricted ordinary pedestrians and vehicles at San Antonio’s access to the Simón Bolívar bridge on 26–27 July 2025 for municipal-election security. Medical patients, ambulance transfers and repatriation movements could still pass. Barriers were removed on the morning of 28 July; broader announcements of strict controls covered different dates and do not establish an identical closure at every border post.

verification.notes: Precise local July26 onset used rather than broader July25 controls; humanitarian passage preserved.

summary: Suriname’s maritime authority prohibited the Canawaima ferry from sailing from 22 August 2026 because of safety deficiencies, interrupting the Moleson Creek–South Drain link with Guyana. The restriction was lifted and ferry operations resumed on 28 August. Immigration processing for small-boat passengers continued during the suspension, so the measure did not close the entire Corentyne River frontier.

verification.notes: Regulatory ferry ban distinguished from other boats, earlier outage and later provisional authorization.

summary: Authorities scheduled the La Gabrielle ferry between Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni and Albina to stop from 25 September through 30 October 2017 for maintenance and repairs. Later official notices indicate service was available by December and announce additional holiday sailings. They do not confirm the first reopening or adherence to the planned maintenance dates, and the announcement did not suspend private boats or all river crossings.

verification.notes: Planned inclusive maintenance window preserved; later availability not October31 reopening proof.
